newsitem.title: USA: U.S. and pulp firm strike deal on Tongass timber.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and pulp firm strike deal on Tongass timber.

text.p: The U.S. Forest Service said Friday it will supply timber from Alaska's Tongass National Forest over the next three years to two sawmills operated by Louisiana-Pacific Corp. that employ some 400 people, keeping them running.

The government will also pay Louisiana-Pacific subsidiary Ketchikan Pulp Corp. $140 million to settle all the company's claims over alleged violations of a controversial, 50-year timber supply contract, the Forest Service said.
The Forest Service will provide 300 million board feet of timber to the two mills.

In exchange, Ketchikan Pulp has promised to maintain targeted employment levels and to be responsible for environmental cleanup at various sites, including a cove that has been used for decades for dumping wastes from the company's aged Ketchikan, Alaska, pulp mill.

The deal followed four months of negotiations that began when Ketchikan Pulp and Lousiana-Pacific announced plans to shut down the huge pulp mill. The mill, long one of southeast Alaska's top employers, is scheduled for closure in March.
Ketchikan Pulp and its corporate owner blamed the impending closure on the federal government's failure to extend and expand the controversial 50-year timber supply contract.
But the Clinton administration argued that closure of the pulp mill violated terms of the 50-year contract, effectively cancelling it.
Representatives of opposing sides in the dispute said Friday's agreement eased the effects of the pulp mill closure.

"While no agreement could erase the difficulties caused by the loss of a major employer, this agreement will help protect jobs and permit a smooth transition to future management of the Tongass National Forest," Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said in a news release.
Louisiana-Pacific Chairman Mark Suwyn also hailed the agreement.

"Fortunately, both sides had the same objective in mind, namely to preserve the sawmill operations for the immediate future. Those two mills and the associated forestry operations employ about 400 men and women and are an important element of the southeast Alaska economy," Suwyn said in a statement.
Louisiana-Pacific said the pledge of timber supply for the sawmills preserves an economic value of $20 million to $35 million for Ketchikan Pulp.
Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles said the deal will help pave the way to a more modern timber industry in southeast Alaska.
The 50-year timber supply contract was born in the 1950s, when the federal government was seeking to encourage settlement and industrialisation of southeast Alaska.
The contract has been criticised by environmentalists and economists, who characterise it as a government subsidy that damages the largest U.S. national forest.
